Full layouts, sizes, offsets and alignment of per-CPU data, hierarchy node and callback objects.
Implementation and ordering guarantees of node, outer, bypass, group and barrier guards beyond the assertions observed.

findings.text: Tree RCU exposes a global barrier operation that does not return until every callback queued before entry has executed. Concurrent callers serialize on a dedicated mutex with early exit if a peer completed equivalent work. The operation drives per-CPU coverage, waits on a completion, then closes the sequence and publishes updated snapshots.

Tiny RCU exposes a barrier operation with the same completion contract as the tree variant but realized as a single grace-period wait using the expedited flavor. No per-CPU dispatch or explicit counting is visible in this configuration.

A global lazy-flush interval controls how long lazy-only bypass content may age before flushing. One interface reads the current interval and a companion interface updates it. The value is consumed by bypass flush decisions and by deferred wakeup timing.
An async helper reports whether lazy handling must be hurried. It indicates hurry when lazy support is compiled out or when a nesting counter shows an active hurry section.

Each hierarchy node maintains an overload mask with one bit per grouped CPU. The bit reflects whether that CPU main queue length reaches a global threshold. A non-positive threshold disables the mechanism for early boot. The fast path avoids locking when the bit already matches the threshold comparison.
A CPU counts as online for barrier purposes when its group bit intersects the node onboarding mask. The mask is sampled with a single atomic read and never modified by the predicate itself.

Main queue length accounting includes bypass-resident callbacks. Length is incremented before bypass insertion so concurrent observers never see an entry without its count. A flush moves all bypass content plus an optional newcomer into the main pending set and resets the lazy count and the bypass age stamp.

Offloaded queue protection uses two levels. The outer list guard is taken only when offload is enabled and requires interrupts disabled. The bypass guard is separate and also requires interrupts disabled, acquired with a fast attempt and expected to contend only between local enqueue and remote flush. Flush paths require the outer guard and then acquire the bypass guard internally.

Hierarchy node updates occur under the node guard with an assertion that the guard is held. Opportunistic advance uses a try acquisition and never blocks. Barrier entrainment requires the barrier guard. Group wakeup state including sleep flag, deferred level and timer is protected by the group leader guard, and deferred cancellation expects that guard to be held.

Enqueue for offloaded CPUs selects among direct main-queue insertion, bypass insertion that absorbs the newcomer, or bypass flush followed by either absorption or delegation back to direct insertion. Selection depends on offload enablement, scheduler running state, per-interval direct-enqueue quota, laziness of the newcomer, and bypass size or age. The boolean result tells the caller whether further enqueue work remains.

Grace-period thread wakeup distinguishes poll mode, missing thread, previously empty versus non-empty queues, lazy-only bypass content, and caller interrupt state. Empty-to-nonempty transitions either wake immediately, schedule a deferred timer, or use a longer lazy delay. Immediate wake clears a sleep indicator under the group guard and signals a wait queue after release, while any deferred arm is cancelled before an immediate wake.

The tree barrier progresses through snapshot, mutex serialization, sequence start, per-CPU coverage, completion wait, sequence end, and snapshot publication. Per-CPU coverage is reached by skipping already-covered CPUs, marking empty queues, entraining offline CPUs locally, or dispatching a handler to online CPUs with retry on failure. Completion counting starts with a bias to avoid premature zero.

Bypass flush need is a pure function of current bypass size, lazy subset size, age stamp and current time. Empty bypass never needs flush. Size at or above a high-water threshold forces flush, with a doubled threshold when not in hurried mode. Otherwise age beyond a timeout forces flush, where lazy-only content uses the configurable lazy interval and mixed content uses a shorter interval depending on hurry.
Wakeup of a grace-period related thread is conditional on target validity and yielding state. A yielding thread is only woken from idle context, while non-yielding threads may be woken generally.

Callback advancement without wakeup is purely opportunistic. It proceeds only when list protection is already held, a grace period is in progress, and the node guard can be acquired without blocking. The grace period is guaranteed not to close while the node guard is held.
Direct enqueue appends to the per-CPU segmented list and emits callback and segment statistics traces. It assumes the caller already holds the protection required for the chosen configuration.

Observed per-CPU state includes a main segmented queue, a bypass queue with length and lazy length, first-enqueue stamp, per-interval quota counters, outer and bypass guards, group leader pointer with group guard wait queue sleep flag deferred level and timer, thread pointer, hierarchy node pointer with group mask, and barrier snapshot. Observed node state includes overload mask, onboarding masks and grace sequence. No complete layout or offsets are visible here.

Scale test initialization validates lazy timing before starting workers. It temporarily lengthens the lazy interval, drains prior work, enqueues one probe, waits for its completion flag, checks that elapsed time falls within an expected window, restores the interval, then creates worker and expedited threads and waits for startup. Failures unwind through a common cleanup path.

The lazy probe uses a dedicated callback object, a timestamp variable capturing execution time, and a flag variable recording invocation. The probe handler records time and sets the flag once per invocation.

In configurations without offload support the outer guards are no-operations, flush reports success without action, wake reports no wake, and the enqueue and wake helpers are unreachable dead code guarded by a one-time warning.

Several paths emit one-time warnings for unexpected states rather than correcting them: bypass contention from a remote CPU, bypass content during early boot or after a flush that should have drained it, unexpected invocation of dead code, and barrier snapshot mismatches after entrainment or dispatch. Callers must treat these as diagnostic signals of logic violations.

Barrier tracing records a textual phase label together with target CPU, current completion count and sequence value. It is invoked at phase transitions and per-CPU decisions and has no effect on barrier correctness.
